subject: Automotive & EVs
title: The Baker Electric
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Baker Electric usable.

hook.text: The Baker Electric was the luxury EV of the early 1900s—elegant, silent, and extremely expensive.

buildup.text: It had a range of 50–100 miles, plush interiors, and was marketed directly to wealthy women.

discovery.text: Owners included Thomas Edison's wife, Clara Ford, and several First Ladies of the United States.

twist.text: But at $2,800 it cost four times more than a Model T. Only the rich could afford one.

climax.text: Baker stopped making cars by 1916 as gas vehicles got cheaper and more practical for everyone.

punchline.text: The first premium EV brand was a century ahead of its time.

details.summary: The Baker Electric was one of the most popular cars in America from 1899 to 1914, favored by women and urban drivers for its quiet operation, clean running, and easy starting compared to cranky gasoline cars.
details.whyItMatters: The Baker Electric shows that electric cars were mainstream transportation over a century ago. Its decline was not due to inferior technology but to gasoline's expanding range and the electric starter motor.
takeaways: Baker Electrics were popular urban cars in the early 1900s
They were marketed to women as clean and easy to operate
The electric starter motor for gas cars eliminated one of their key advantages

faq.question: Why were electric cars marketed specifically to women?
faq.answer: Gasoline cars required hand-cranking to start, which was physically demanding and could result in broken arms from kickback. Electric cars started with a switch, making them much more accessible regardless of physical strength.

faq.question: What killed the Baker Electric and other early EVs?
faq.answer: Charles Kettering's electric starter motor for gas cars in 1912, Henry Ford's cheap Model T, and the expansion of roads beyond city limits all combined to eliminate the advantages electric cars once held.
